title: Saakhi
author: Kabirdas
tagline: Kabir’s couplets against empty ritual: the guru before God, the narrow lane of love, and the seven seas as ink.

overview.intro: A sakhi is a short, proverb-like couplet in which Kabir packs a whole argument. The Sahitya Sagar selection gathers several sakhis rather than one continuous poem, and they share a single thread: genuine spiritual understanding cannot be reduced to outward religious display. Kabir gives the guru precedence over God, insists that the ego and the divine cannot share one heart, questions shouting at God from a mosque roof, turns the logic of stone-worship back on itself, and closes by saying that even seven seas of ink could not record God’s qualities. The force of the form is its compression — a couplet that can be recited, remembered and argued with.

learn.title: What a sakhi is, and how the selection is built

blocks.text: A sakhi is a witness-statement in verse: two compact lines that deliver a complete judgement. Kabir uses the form as a teacher uses a maxim — small enough to carry, sharp enough to cut. Because each couplet stands alone, the Sahitya Sagar selection can gather several sakhis without a narrative thread; what binds them is a shared concern. Read them as a group of arguments about the same problem: how devotion differs from the performance of religion.

The diction matters as much as the argument. Kabir writes in a mixed vernacular that draws on several regional speech forms, deliberately avoiding the polished register of courtly poetry. That choice is itself part of his position: he speaks in the language of ordinary people, and he refuses the ornament that might make his message decorative rather than true.

items: Guru and God stand together, and the speaker asks whose feet to touch first; he honours the guru, who showed him God.
When "I" was present, Hari was not; now Hari is present and "I" is not — love’s lane is too narrow for two.
Kabir questions the need to call out to God from a mosque roof, using a pointed question to puncture outward display.
If worshiping a stone alone brought God, a mountain would be more worthy; the working millstone that feeds people is the truer object of respect.
Even with the seven seas as ink and the earth as paper, God’s qualities cannot all be written.

blocks.text: Notice how the couplets escalate. The first two establish a hierarchy — guru over God, God over ego. The next two attack the logic of empty ritual by following it to its absurd conclusion. The last widens the frame entirely: no praise is adequate, so all the show of religion is beside the point. The sequence moves from instruction to satire to awe.

blocks.text: Kabir’s chief technique is compression. He rarely explains; he asserts, questions or contrasts, and trusts the reader to complete the thought. The result is a poetry of pressure rather than description, where a single image — the narrow lane, the millstone, the seas of ink — carries an entire theology.

learn.title: Themes: ego, the guru, and devotion without display

blocks.caption: What Kabir values against what he rejects
rows: Love’s lane is too narrow for two
Sacred objects valued only as objects

blocks.text: The selection’s deepest theme is that devotion is a condition of the heart, not a display before the world. Kabir does not reject religion; he rejects the substitution of ritual for understanding. Beneath that runs his respect for the guru, the one human figure who can point the way, and his insistence that true merit lies in humility and service rather than in status or show.

Kabir wrote from the weaver’s workshop, not the priest’s chair, and his sakhis belong to the nirgun strand of bhakti, which seeks a formless divine rather than a personal deity worshipped through images and offices. That background explains his impatience with external display: for a nirgun poet, the divine is not located in a temple, a mosque or a stone, so religion that stops at those places has missed its object entirely.

It also explains the accessibility of the form. A couplet can be learned by a labourer and debated by a scholar; Kabir’s choice of the sakhi lets his argument travel. Centuries later the same couplets are still quoted as proverbs, which is exactly the afterlife their form was built for.

Examinations on this selection usually ask for the central idea, an explanation of one or two couplets, or a note on Kabir’s language. In every case, quote the couplet’s sense precisely, then paraphrase and interpret. Kabir’s compressed lines punish vagueness: an answer that says "Kabir talks about God" earns little, while one that explains the narrow lane or the millstone logic earns full marks.

items: Learn the guru-first couplet and the "I/Hari" couplet well enough to paraphrase them accurately.
Explain the stone-worship logic step by step — the absurd conclusion is the argument.
Name the language deliberately: mixed vernacular, plain and unornamented, chosen to match the message.

figures.caption: Figure: The selection’s five arguments in sequence
figures.description: A left-to-right chain of five linked panels: (1) Guru and God stand together, guru honoured; (2) "I" and Hari cannot share the narrow lane; (3) the question of shouting from a mosque roof; (4) the stone, the mountain and the working millstone; (5) seven seas as ink, the earth as paper, and qualities that cannot be written. An arrow beneath labels the movement: instruction → satire → awe.

figures.caption: Figure: Devotion inward, ritual outward
figures.description: A split diagram. Left column, "What Kabir values": the guru, humility, the emptied ego, sincere inward devotion, usefulness. Right column, "What he rejects": pride, the swelling of "I", shouted performance, sacred objects treated as ends. Arrows cross out the right column’s items in the order the couplets attack them.

keyPoints: A sakhi is a two-line proverb-like couplet; the selection is a group of them, not one continuous poem.
The guru-first couplet gives the guru precedence because the guru revealed God to the seeker.
The "I and Hari" couplet is a paradox: as the ego recedes, the divine becomes present.
"Love’s lane is too narrow for two" means ego and devotion cannot occupy one heart together.
The mosque-roof couplet is a rhetorical question attacking outward, shouted religious display.
The stone-worship couplet uses absurd logic: if stone alone saved, a mountain would save more.
The millstone matters because it is useful — it feeds people — which Kabir sets above sacred objects.
The closing hyperbole of seven seas as ink admits that no praise, however vast, is adequate.
Kabir’s mixed vernacular is plain and unornamented by design, matching his refusal of religious decoration.
examFocus: Central idea: genuine devotion is inward and humble; it cannot be replaced by ritual, display or status.

questions.prompt: In the first sakhi, whose feet does Kabir choose to touch first?
options: The guru’s, because the guru showed him God
questions.answer: The guru’s, because the guru showed him God
questions.explanation: Guru and God stand together, and Kabir honours the guru first — balihari to the guru, who revealed Govind to him.
questions.commonMistake: Kabir does not rank God lower; he honours the guru as the one who made God known.

questions.prompt: What does the image of the narrow lane of love suggest?
options: Ego and devotion cannot both occupy the heart
The path to God is physically long
Love is difficult for the poor
questions.answer: Ego and devotion cannot both occupy the heart
questions.explanation: The lane is so narrow that two cannot fit: as the swelling "I" recedes, Hari becomes present. The image compresses a whole teaching about selflessness.
questions.commonMistake: It is not about physical distance but about the incompatibility of ego and the divine.

questions.prompt: Which device dominates the mosque-roof couplet?
options: A rhetorical question challenging outward display
A simile comparing God to light
questions.answer: A rhetorical question challenging outward display
questions.explanation: Kabir asks why one must call out to God from a mosque roof; the question is not seeking information but puncturing the idea that loud, public worship is truer worship.
questions.commonMistake: The couplet attacks performance, not the mosque itself.

questions.prompt: Why does Kabir value the millstone over a stone idol?
options: Because it is useful — it feeds people
Because it is made of finer stone
questions.answer: Because it is useful — it feeds people
questions.explanation: Kabir follows the logic of stone-worship to its absurd conclusion: if any stone were sacred, a mountain would outrank an idol; but the working millstone, which feeds people, deserves the greater respect.
questions.commonMistake: The point is usefulness and service, not size or sanctity of material.

questions.prompt: What does the closing sakhi say about writing God’s qualities?
questions.answer: That even with the seven seas as ink and the whole earth as paper, God’s qualities could never all be written.
questions.explanation: The deliberate hyperbole admits the inadequacy of all praise, and so quietly dismisses the whole apparatus of religious show as beside the point.
questions.commonMistake: Present it as an exaggeration with a purpose, not as a factual claim about ink and paper.

questions.prompt: What kind of language does Kabir use, and why does it suit his message?
questions.answer: He uses a plain mixed vernacular (sadhukkadi or panchmel diction), which suits his message because it keeps his teaching accessible to ordinary people and refuses decorative, courtly ornament.
questions.explanation: The form matches the content: a poet attacking religious decoration chooses a language that is itself unornamented and drawn from everyday speech.
questions.commonMistake: Name the diction precisely rather than calling it simply "simple Hindi".

questions.prompt: Explain the couplet in which "I" and Hari cannot both be present, and its significance.
questions.answer: Kabir says that when the ego — the swelling sense of "I" — was present, Hari was not, and now that Hari is present, "I" is not, because love’s lane is too narrow for two. The paradox is deliberate: the self must empty before the divine can enter. Its significance is theological as well as practical — for a nirgun bhakti poet, devotion is not an addition to the ego but its replacement, and humility is not a polite manner but a precondition of genuine spiritual life.
questions.explanation: Paraphrase the couplet first, then name the paradox and unpack why ego and devotion are mutually exclusive in Kabir’s thought.
questions.commonMistake: Do not read it as self-hatred; the point is selflessness, not contempt for the self.

questions.prompt: How does the stone-worship sakhi use logic to make its point?
questions.answer: It grants the premise of stone-worship and then follows it to an absurd conclusion: if worshiping a stone alone could bring God, then a whole mountain would be more powerful still — yet the millstone that feeds people is the truer object of respect.
questions.explanation: Kabir does not argue directly against the practice; he exposes it by taking it further than its defenders intend, which is more persuasive than a flat denial.
questions.commonMistake: Describe the step-by-step logic; saying "Kabir dislikes idols" misses the argumentative method.

questions.prompt: Describe the Sahitya Sagar Saakhi selection and show how its couplets share one central thread.
questions.answer: The selection gathers several short sakhi couplets rather than one continuous poem, each a complete judgement in two lines. The first gives the guru precedence over God, because the guru revealed God to the seeker. The second is a paradox: when "I" was present Hari was not, and now that Hari is present "I" am not, for love’s lane is too narrow for two. The third questions the need to shout at God from a mosque roof, using a rhetorical question to puncture outward display. The fourth follows stone-worship to its absurd conclusion, ranking the feeding millstone above any idol. The last widens the frame, imagining the seven seas as ink and the earth as paper, still unequal to writing God’s qualities. The single thread is that genuine devotion is inward, humble and free of display: it cannot be reduced to ritual, status or performance. Kabir’s plain mixed vernacular suits this message, refusing the ornament that might make religion decorative rather than true.
questions.explanation: Move couplet by couplet, then name the shared thread explicitly; the question asks for both the description and the argument that binds it.
questions.commonMistake: Do not treat the sakhis as unrelated verses — the shared thread is what earns the marks.

questions.prompt: Does Kabir reject religion, or only its empty forms? Discuss with reference to the sakhis.
questions.answer: Kabir does not reject devotion — he repeatedly honours the guru and speaks with awe of God’s unwriteable qualities. What he rejects is the substitution of outward performance for inward understanding: shouting from a roof, worshipping a stone as though the divine resided in it, pride in religious status. The stone-worship couplet is revealing, because it defends usefulness and service rather than abandoning the sacred altogether. A reader today can hear the same critique wherever ritual is treated as a substitute for conduct. Kabir’s position is therefore not irreligion but a demand that devotion be measured by humility and service rather than by display.
questions.explanation: Take a clear position, then support it with the couplets that praise (the guru, God’s qualities) and those that satirise (the mosque roof, the idol), showing that the target is form, not faith.
questions.commonMistake: Do not call Kabir an atheist; the text’s reverence is unmistakable.
